title: What If You Were Born as Lucky Luciano? | The New York Mob

paras: If you were born as Lucky Luciano, you'd be thrown in a car, beaten, cut, and dumped on a beach.
And you'd walk away.
You'd remove the two most powerful bosses in New York in five months.
Then rebuild the whole Mafia like a company, with a board.
And the country you built it in?
It puts you on a ship.
And sends you away for good.
But right now?
You're a baby in a Sicilian mining town.
No money. No gang. Not even the name Lucky.
You're born Salvatore Lucania, on November 24th, 1897, in Lercara Friddi.
The hills around town are full of sulfur.
Your father, Antonio, works the mines.
Your mother, Rosalia, keeps the house running on almost nothing.
You have two big brothers, Giuseppe and Bartolomeo.
Two little sisters will come later.
And every family on your street dreams about the same place.
America.
In 1906, the dream comes true.
You're eight. Some say nine.
The whole family crosses the ocean by ship.
Remember that ship.
New York hits you like a wall.
You end up on the Lower East Side of Manhattan.
Five-story tenements. Laundry lines. A dozen languages on every corner.
Your father works hard and earns little.
You watch him come home tired every night.
And you decide something very early.
You are not going to live like that.
At fourteen, you quit school.
You get a job delivering hats.
Seven dollars a week.
Then one day you roll dice in the street.
And you win two hundred and forty-four dollars.
That's about eight months of hats.
You quit on the spot.
Remember the dice.
Your parents send you to the Brooklyn Truancy School.
It doesn't fix anything.
You come out with a business idea.
The Jewish kids in the neighborhood get beaten up by Italian and Irish gangs.
So you sell them protection.
Ten cents a week. Pay, and nobody touches you.
Don't pay, and the person who touches you is you.
Then one skinny kid looks up at you and says no.
He's tiny. He's outnumbered. He doesn't blink.
His name is Meyer Lansky.
Instead of beating him, you make him your friend.
Remember the kid who said no.
In 1916 you're eighteen, and you're caught selling heroin.
It's the first time they lock you up.
It won't be the last.
In 1920, America bans alcohol.
And overnight, a whole country becomes your customer.
You run with Frank Costello and Vito Genovese.
And you find a teacher. Arnold Rothstein, the gambler they say fixed the World Series.
He teaches you that bootlegging isn't a street crime.
It's a business.
He teaches you how to dress. How to eat. How to talk to rich people.
He even takes you shopping for suits.
Then the biggest boss in New York hires you.
Giuseppe Masseria. Joe the Boss.
You start as his gunman.
You end up as his right hand.
By the mid-twenties, the story goes, your rackets bring in twelve million dollars a year.
October 1929. You're on a Manhattan street at night.
A car pulls up. A gun. You get in.
They beat you. They cut your face.
And at six in the morning, a cop finds you bleeding near Huguenot Beach, on Staten Island.
You still have three hundred dollars in a hidden pocket.
So it wasn't a robbery.
Who did it? You tell the police you have no idea.
Later, you blame the cops. Others blame a rival boss.
Nobody agrees.
You keep a scar on your chin.
And a right eye that droops for years.
And the name everyone uses now? Lucky.
Some say it's because you survived the ride.
Some say it's the dice.
Some say you had it long before.
Remember the dice?
Even your nickname is a gamble.
Quick pause.
A lot of you asked for a mob boss, so here's the man who built the modern Mafia.
Who should live next? Leave a name in the comments.
And if you want a new life every day, subscribe.
By 1930, the mob in New York is at war.
Masseria on one side.
On the other, an old-school Sicilian boss named Salvatore Maranzano.
Bodies pile up on both sides. And you're stuck in the middle.
So you make a quiet deal with the other side.
End the war. Remove Joe the Boss.
April 15th, 1931. A restaurant on Coney Island.
You and Masseria eat lunch.
Then you play cards.
The story goes, you get up to use the bathroom.
While you're gone, four men walk in and open fire.
Masseria dies at the table.
You come out, and the war is over.
Just like that.
Maranzano wins.
He splits New York into five families.
And he crowns himself boss of all bosses.
By late summer, you hear he's hired a killer.
For you.
September 10th, 1931.
Men with badges walk into Maranzano's office on Park Avenue.
They say they're government agents.
They're not.
They're Jewish gangsters, sent with help from your oldest friend.
Remember the kid who said no?
Meyer Lansky just said yes.
Maranzano is stabbed and shot in his own office.
And you're the most powerful man in the underworld.
You're thirty-three.
But you don't take the crown.
You get rid of it.
No more boss of bosses.
Instead, the families get a Commission. A board. A vote.
You turned the Mafia into a company.
And you're the chairman.
You live in a suite at the Waldorf-Astoria.
Expensive suits. Nightclubs. Racetracks.
Life is good.
Then a young prosecutor named Thomas Dewey starts hunting the mob.
A gangster called Dutch Schultz wants to kill him.
The Commission says no.
Schultz says he'll do it anyway.
So in October 1935, Schultz gets shot in a Newark restaurant.
You just saved the life of the man who's coming for you.
Dewey raids two hundred brothels in a single sweep.
Then he charges you with running them.
You run to Hot Springs, Arkansas.
They drag you back.
In June 1936, a jury finds you guilty.
Thirty to fifty years.
Later, some of the witnesses take back what they said.
Too late.
Years later, you'll say it in one line.
Dewey framed me.
They send you to Clinton Prison, in Dannemora.
Way up north, near Canada.
People call it Little Siberia.
In 1942, America is at war.
In New York harbor, a huge French liner called the Normandie catches fire and rolls over.
The Navy panics. Sabotage, on the docks?
And the docks belong to the mob.
So naval intelligence does something it will keep quiet for years.
It talks to Meyer Lansky.
And Lansky talks to you.
You're moved to a softer prison.
Word goes out. The waterfront stays quiet.
Some say you even helped the invasion of Sicily.
How much you really helped? Nobody agrees.
In January 1946, Governor Dewey, the same man who sent you away, commutes your sentence.
On one condition.
You leave America forever.
February 1946. A ship called the Laura Keene, in Brooklyn.
Remember the ship that brought you here?
This one only goes one way.
But you're not done.
By the end of 1946, you're secretly in Havana, Cuba.
Ninety miles from Florida.
The bosses fly in to meet you at the Hotel Nacional.
Washington finds out.
And Cuba sends you back to Italy.
You settle in Naples.
You fall in love with a dancer named Igea Lissoni.
Police follow you everywhere.
Reporters ask you about New York.
You tell one of them you almost made Dewey president.
January 26th, 1962. Capodichino airport, Naples.
You're waiting for a man named Martin Gosch.
He wants to tell your story. A film, or a book. Nobody agrees which.
Your heart stops before he arrives.
You're sixty-four.
America won't let you in alive.
But it lets you come home now.
You're buried in Saint John Cemetery, in Queens, New York.
You lost your freedom for ten years.
You were thrown out of two countries.
And you never set foot in New York again while you were breathing.
But you walked away from a beach where you should have died.
You ended a war with a trip to the bathroom.
And the system you built still has your fingerprints on it.
So tell me.
Did Lucky Luciano really help win a war, or did he just talk his way out of prison?
